title: multi-gpu-serving-design-scheduling-kv-cache-draft
content:
Purpose:

This is a working draft for the Multi-GPU serving design focusing on kernels, scheduling, KV cache management, tensor/pipeline parallelism, NCCL tuning, and parameter/optimizer sharding. Goal: produce a practical, measurable design that we can prototype in the next 6-8 weeks and evaluate against our latency/throughput SLOs for both hosted and Dedicated deployments.

High-level goals and constraints:
- Support both high-throughput batch workloads and low-latency single-request streaming.
- Minimize cross-GPU stalls and NCCL synchronization overhead while keeping model semantics identical to single-GPU outputs.
- Support graceful degradation: if a GPU or link fails, degrade to a cheaper variant or fall back to local single-GPU execution without catastrophic tail-latency spikes.
- Keep memory overhead for KV caches predictable; enable sharded KV caches across GPUs for very long context lengths.
- Avoid complex customer-facing configuration where possible; provide sane defaults and telemetry-driven tuning.

Design options considered (summary):
1) Pure tensor-parallel (TP) serving:
   - Partition model tensors across GPUs (e.g., 8-way TP for LLM weights). Each micro-batch is executed in lockstep; heavy NCCL AllReduce/AllGather at every layer.
   - Pros: simple mapping to existing TP runtimes; supports models that already have TP checkpoints.
   - Cons: high synchronization cost per layer, poor tail latency for single-request scenarios, requires careful NCCL tuning.

2) Pipeline-parallel (PP) serving with micro-batching:
   - Split model into pipeline stages across GPUs. Use micro-batching and pipeline schedules (1F1B etc.).
   - Pros: better utilization at large batch sizes, can reduce per-layer NCCL chatter.
   - Cons: increases latency for single-request streaming unless we use model parallel prefixes or speculative execution. Complexity in dynamic batching.

3) Hybrid TP+PP (recommended for many production cases):
   - Combine coarse-grained pipeline stages (e.g., 2-4 stages) with tensor-parallelism inside each stage. Reduces cross-node communication; fewer pipeline stages means less bubble overhead.
   - Pros: balance of latency and throughput; reuses TP-optimized kernels inside stage; easier to implement KV cache sharding per stage.
   - Cons: more complex orchestration; placement/partitioning heuristics required.

4) Sharded-weight + optimizer-state approach for very large models (ZeRO-style) for Private Dedicated/On-prem:
   - Shard parameters/optimizer state across GPUs to reduce per-GPU memory footprint. For inference-only, we shard weights and optionally cache frequently used slices locally.
   - Pros: supports very large models on limited hardware.
   - Cons: complexity around serving-time parameter access; potential throughput impact if many remote reads are necessary.

Recommendation (initial prototype): Hybrid TP+PP with sharded KV cache and NCCL tuning per topology. Rationale: best balance for our mixed workloads and matches many customer needs (latency-sensitive chat + throughput scoring).

Key components and responsibilities:
- Placement & Partitioning service (or offline planner): decides how to split layers into pipeline stages and how many TP ranks per stage. Inputs: model size, layer compute cost, customer latency SLO, available GPU topology (nodes, NVLinks). Output: placement plan (stage boundaries, rank groups).

- Runtime scheduler (per-serving-pod): manages micro-batching, request routing to stages, scheduling of forward passes, prioritization, backpressure handling, and fallback logic.

- KV cache manager: responsible for caching key/value tensors for past tokens. Needs to handle sharding, eviction, remote fetch, and local prefetching.

- NCCL tuning & comm-layer: a thin abstraction to select transport (NVLink/PCIe/IB), algorithm (Ring/Tree/LL/LL128), and to set per-collective parameters (e.g., NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE, NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING). Exposes per-topology profiles.

Kernels and compute optimizations:
- Use fused attention kernels with prepended rotary/rope and fused softmax+dropout where possible. Provide fallbacks to non-fused ops for unusual sequence lengths.
- Support flash attention or cuDNN/CUTLASS-based custom kernels depending on GPU generation. Heuristics choose kernel based on sequence length, head count, dtype, and whether it’s causal.
- KV cache friendly memory layout: store KV in contiguous blocks per layer per rank with metadata headers for quick offset calculation. Avoid per-token heap allocations in hot path.
- Continuous batching: maintain a small pool of active micro-batches per stage to reduce idle time when waiting for preceding/following stages.

KV cache sharding strategy:
- Per-stage sharding: each pipeline stage owns KV cache for layers in that stage. Within stage, TP ranks shard the KV cache horizontally (by head or by embedding slice) to keep per-GPU memory bounded.
- Addressing reads/writes:
  - Write path (append new tokens): the rank owning the layer appends local KV entries; metadata updated in shared in-memory index.
  - Read path (during next forward): each rank reads local shard; ranks exchange small pointers/offsets if cross-rank dependencies exist (should be rare if sharding chosen carefully).
- Eviction policy: time-based + LRU for interactive workloads. For very long contexts, allow customer-configurable window + async checkpointing of older KV to host or SSD.
- Remote KV access fallback: if a requested KV slice is on another node, we attempt async prefetch via low-latency RDMA/NVLink. If unavailable, fallback to re-computation of prefix (expensive) or a degraded model variant.

NCCL and communication tuning notes:
- Topology awareness: detect NVLink islands, inter-node IB or Ethernet, and choose collectives accordingly. Prefer intra-node NVLink Ring/LL128 for AllGather and AllReduce when available. For cross-node, evaluate NCCL Tree or hierarchical AllReduce to reduce cross-node traffic.
- Per-collective algorithm selection: provide profiles (low-latency vs high-throughput). For latency SLOs (single-request streaming), use algorithms with lower startup latency even if throughput slightly worse. For batch scoring, pick throughput-optimized algos.
- Environment tuning knobs to expose in profiles:
  - NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE (GROUP|PARALLEL)
  - NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING
  - NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT, NCCL_DEBUG=INFO for debug profiles
  - CUDA stream priorities: prioritize control/communication streams in low-latency mode.
- Retry and health policies: monitor NCCL errors, fallback to reconfigure communicator, and surface telemetry (counts of NCCL timeouts, retries) to Console.

Scheduling details:
- Request admission: prioritize small interactive requests with a soft real-time queue. Larger scoring batches go to a lower priority queue.
- Dynamic micro-batching: pack compatible requests (same model/version, same generation parameters) into micro-batches up to per-stage target size. For streaming, allow micro-batches of size 1 with preferential scheduling.
- Backpressure: if a downstream stage is saturated, upstream stages must stall or buffer a configurable number of micro-batches. Avoid unbounded buffering.
- Preemption: implement light-weight preemption of low-priority micro-batches in favor of latency-critical work. Preemption should be cooperative (drain current op in kernel-friendly boundary).

Failure modes and graceful degradation:
- Link/node failure during AllGather/AllReduce: detect and reconfigure communicator; if reconfiguration would breach latency SLO, fall back to local single-GPU execution for a short period and route new requests accordingly.
- KV cache inconsistency: version the KV cache by request-id; when a mismatch is detected, invalidate and re-warm from prefix where possible.

Operational plan and telemetry:
- Key metrics to capture:
  - per-stage GPU utilization, per-call latency P50/P95/P99, NCCL collective latency histogram, NVLink throughput, number of remote KV fetches, KV cache hit rate, memory per-GPU (weights + KV + optimizer state), micro-batch formation rate, preemption counts.
- Automated experiments:
  - Bump TP degree: measure per-layer AllReduce vs compute overlap and end-to-end latency.
  - Vary pipeline stage splits: 1 vs 2 vs 4 stages, measure bubble overhead and tail-latency for streaming.
  - Try different NCCL algos and record end-to-end stats under mixed traffic.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Placement heuristics: need an automated cost model for splitting layers into stages that considers NVLink topology. Action: Ravi to draft cost model (ENG-4721).
- KV cache addressability: evaluate tradeoffs of sharding by head vs embedding slice vs token-range. Quick prototype: head-based sharding for transformers with equal head sizes.
- Failure recovery semantics: define maximum acceptable degrade-to-single-node window for dedicated deployments under SLA.
- Profiling harness: build microbench scripts to measure AllGather/AllReduce latency vs payload for our supported GPU families (A100, H100, L40).

Prototype plan (6-8 weeks):
- Week 1-2: implement placement planner + prototype hybrid mapping for a small Llama-like model.
- Week 3-4: implement KV cache sharding (head-based) and local shard storage layout.
- Week 5: integrate NCCL profiles and run synthetic perf matrix across topologies.
- Week 6-8: end-to-end prototype on a 4xA100 node and 8xH100 single-node cluster. Collect metrics and iterate.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an engineering-first draft; expect gaps and TODOs. Focus review on correctness of failure modes and the practicality of the prototype plan.
- If you have measured microbench results for specific kernel variants or NCCL profiles, paste them into the linked PR or add as a comment in the Google doc.
